1:
The book closes on a note of empire, and the witnesses open with the tribute Ahasuerus lays "on the land, and upon the isles of the sea." The reformed John Gill takes the phrase to gather in all the king's dominions, both on the continent and on the sea — the Aegean — though he preserves Aben Ezra's alternative, that the words rather describe peoples not under Persian government but standing in fear of it, from whom the king exacted his due. As for why the levy was imposed, Gill offers two conjectures: if Ahasuerus was Xerxes, his exchequer may have been drained by his wars with the Greeks; or the verse may record his renewing the taxes and tribute he had remitted upon his marriage to Esther.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the notice as a measure of the king's greatness. Ahasuerus held a vast dominion, on the continent and among the islands alike, and from it raised a vast revenue; besides the usual customs the kings of Persia exacted, named in Ezra 4:13, he laid this further tribute to serve some great occasion he had for money. Henry cannot let the point pass without a patriot's aside: happy the island, he says, that pays no tribute but what is laid on it by its own chosen representatives, and is not squeezed by an arbitrary power as some neighbouring nations are.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the geography and raises the harder question of identity. The tribute fell on the hundred and twenty-seven provinces already named in the book, and the "isles of the sea" are probably those of the Aegean, conquered by Darius Hystaspes — whom Calmet, he notes, supposes to be the very Ahasuerus of Esther. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the same king as Xerxes, and finds in the tribute the aftermath of a disaster: the ruinous expedition to Greece had taxed the empire's resources to the utmost, and fresh tribute was needed to fill the exhausted coffers, the more so as a harassing war still dragged on, ten years after Salamis, along the coast of Asia Minor. On the "isles" Ellicott is precise — the chief island still left to Persia was Cyprus, for those in the Aegean were by now free of Persian rule, though he grants the old phrase may simply have been retained out of habit, as later kings were long styled sovereigns of France or of Jerusalem after the lands were lost.

So the witnesses converge on a mighty king pressed for revenue, yet part over who he was — Xerxes, as Gill tentatively and Ellicott confidently hold, or Darius Hystaspes, as Calmet proposed and Clarke reports — and over the isles, whether the lost Aegean or the Cyprus that alone remained.
2:
"Are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?" The witnesses take the closing formula — the acts of the king's power and might, and the record of Mordecai's advancement — and turn it into a meditation on what lasts and what perishes. The reformed John Gill notes only, of "all the acts of his power, and of his might," that Xerxes was indeed a very mighty and powerful prince, whose deeds had filled the royal annals.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses attend both to those chronicles and to their fate. Adam Clarke observes that the Persians were ever remarkable for keeping exact chronicles of all public events; their Tareekhs, compositions of just this kind, remained numerous and important down to his own day. John Wesley looks past the volumes to their vanishing: these chronicles are lost long since and buried in oblivion, while the sacred writings remain throughout the world — for when the kingdoms of men, their monarchs and their monarchies, are destroyed, and their memorial perishes with them, the kingdom of God among men and the records of that kingdom shall remain as the days of heaven.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the same contrast at length. Many more instances of the grandeur of Ahasuerus might have been given, he says, but they were not thought fit to be recorded in the sacred story, which is confined to the Jews and touches other nations only where their affairs fall in with Israel's; those instances were written instead in the Persian chronicles — long since lost and buried in oblivion, while the sacred writings live, live in honour, and will live till time shall be no more. When the kingdoms of men are destroyed and their memorial has perished with them, as in Psalm 9:6, the kingdom of God and its records shall remain and be as the days of heaven, the very promise of Daniel 2:44. The concerns of the despised worshippers of the Lord, Henry marvels, are deemed by the Holy Spirit more important than the exploits of the most illustrious monarch on earth.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a single philological touch: the "power" here named is the same word rendered "authority" where Esther writes to confirm the letter of Purim in Esther 9:29.

The witnesses do not divide. They gather around one confession, drawn from a verse that seems only to defer to a lost royal register: the annals of the greatest empire of the age have crumbled into oblivion, while the brief sacred record of a captive people and their deliverance endures — a quiet parable, in the book's last lines, of whose kingdom and whose memory outlast the years.
3:
The book ends not with the king but with the Jew who had become his right hand, and the witnesses close the chapter on the greatness and goodness of Mordecai. The reformed John Gill states the plain dignity of it: Mordecai was next unto Ahasuerus, the second man in the kingdom, the chief of the counsellors, and prime minister of state. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enlarges the office — Mordecai was prime minister, and under the king governor of the whole empire — and relays the Targum's extravagant encomium, that all the kings of the earth feared and trembled before him, that he shone like the evening star among the stars and beamed like the dawn, and was chief among the kings. On the closing clauses Clarke hears a settled benevolence: in "seeking the wealth of his people" Mordecai studied to promote the Jewish interest to the utmost of his power, and in "speaking peace to all his seed" he laboured to found their prosperity on a basis that might stand for ever.

Clarke marks, too, where the Hebrew ends. Here the Hebrew text closes; but the ancient Vulgate and the Greek add ten verses to this chapter and six whole chapters besides, swelling the book to sixteen chapters — the apocryphal additions on which, he says, it is not his province to comment, this being the last of the historical books before the long silence that runs on to the coming of Christ.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the greatness in history and leaves its end in shadow. The events of the book carry us to about 470 B.C., when Mordecai stood at the zenith of his greatness; how long he held it, and whether death or disgrace brought it down, cannot now be said. All that is known is that near the end of Xerxes' reign the king's favourite and chief adviser was Artabanus, captain of the guard, by whose hand Xerxes was murdered in 464 B.C. The last the sacred record shows of Mordecai, whatever his after-fate, is a man loyal to his people, seeking their weal — their good — and speaking peace to all his seed, all of the stock of Israel.

It is the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry who lingers longest, dividing the verse into greatness and goodness. Mordecai was great: long had he sat contentedly in the king's gate, and now was advanced to the head of the council-board, for men of merit may seem for a time buried alive, yet are often discovered and preferred at last. He was great among the Jews too, dear and familiar to them, so far from envied that they rejoiced in his rise. But his goodness made him truly great, for he did good: he did not disown his people, still writing himself "Mordecai the Jew" and holding to their religion; he sought not his own wealth, as most do who climb to court, but the welfare of his people; he was easy of access and courteous, speaking peace to all; and he took no party against another, but was a common father to them all. One good man in power, blessing a whole people — a fit last word for the book, on which the witnesses gladly rest.
